item.title: A comparative review of implemented explainable AI techniques in multi-agent systems
item.dc:creator: Rahul Kapoor
Nelishia Pillay
item.description:
Authors: Rahul Kapoor, Nelishia Pillay

Abstract Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) has largely been developed for single-model settings, where the target of explanation is one prediction, model, or decision process. This assumption is limited in multi-agent systems (MAS), where outcomes can depend on coordination, communication, decentralised information, and interaction over time. This paper presents a structured comparative review restricted to studies of implemented and empirically evaluated XAI methods in MAS. Here, implemented means that a concrete explanation mechanism is applied in a MAS and tested. The search covered cooperative, competitive, mixed-motive, planning, ad-hoc teamwork, and LLM-based MAS. The included evidence contains work in cooperative and decentralised MARL, as well as planning-oriented and LLM-based MAS work. The review compares studies by explanatory target (the aspect of the system being explained) and stakeholder orientation (who the explanations are for). Current methods can identify influential agents, summarise policies, interpret local decisions, and diagnose failures, however they struggle to explain how interaction and communication produce a system-level outcome. Future work should therefore develop more interaction-aware, empirically grounded, and human-usable explanations for MAS.

item.title: Robin Hood reachability and Büchi bidding games
item.dc:creator: Shaull Almagor
Guy Avni
Neta Dafni
item.description:
Authors: Shaull Almagor, Guy Avni, Neta Dafni

Abstract Two-player graph games are a fundamental model for reasoning about the interaction of agents. These games are played between two players who move a token along a graph. In bidding games, the players have some monetary budget, and at each step they bid for the privilege of moving the token. Typically, the winner of the bid either pays the loser or the bank, or a combination thereof. We introduce Robin Hood bidding games, where at the beginning of every step the richer player pays the poorer a fixed fraction of the difference of their wealth. After the bid, the winner pays the loser. Intuitively, this captures the setting where a regulating entity prevents the accumulation of wealth to some degree. We show that the central property of bidding games, namely the existence of a threshold function, is retained in Robin Hood bidding games for both Reachability and Büchi objectives (in the latter we prove a weaker flavor of threshold). We show that the threshold can be effectively computed (using MILP for reachability objectives, and Linear Real Arithmetic for Büchi objectives). Surprisingly, we show that the games are not always determined exactly at the threshold, unlike their standard counterpart.
